tasks.name: Group Discussion
tasks.description: A structured group discussion where candidates discuss a given topic to assess their ability to communicate ideas, influence others, and work collaboratively. The GTO observes how each candidate contributes, listens, and drives the discussion toward a consensus.
strategy: Open the discussion with a structured approach — define the topic, outline key angles, and invite group input.
Use facts, statistics, and real-world examples to support your points rather than vague opinions.
Actively listen to others and build on their points rather than repeating your own argument.
Maintain eye contact with the group, not just the GTO — you're discussing with peers, not performing.
Summarize the discussion near the end to show leadership and clarity of thought.
commonMistakes: Dominating the discussion without letting others speak — the GTO values cooperation over aggression.
Going off-topic or introducing irrelevant personal anecdotes instead of structured arguments.
Getting into heated arguments or personal attacks when someone disagrees with your point.
Sitting silently and contributing nothing — even quiet candidates must make at least 3-4 meaningful points.
Repeating the same point in different words to fill time instead of adding new substance.
rules: All candidates sit in a semicircle facing each other. The GTO observes from outside.
A topic is given and candidates get 2-3 minutes to think before the discussion begins.
The discussion lasts approximately 20 minutes for 2 topics (10 min each).
No candidate is appointed as leader — the group self-organizes the flow.
Physical gestures like pointing, table-thumping, or standing up are not allowed.

tasks.name: Group Planning Exercise
tasks.description: A complex scenario is presented with multiple problems to solve under time constraints. Candidates individually write their plan, then discuss as a group to arrive at a common solution. Tests planning ability, prioritization, and group consensus-building.
strategy: Read the narrative carefully twice — mark distances, timings, resources, and constraints on the map.
Prioritize problems by severity: life-threatening > time-sensitive > property > convenience.
Create a clear timeline showing who does what and when — use the map to plot movement routes.
Present your individual plan confidently but remain flexible during group discussion.
Volunteer to consolidate the group plan if no one else steps up — it shows initiative and leadership.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the map and distances — your plan must be geographically feasible, not just logical.
Trying to solve every problem simultaneously instead of sequencing tasks by priority.
Being rigid about your individual plan during group discussion and refusing to compromise.
Not accounting for travel time between locations when scheduling tasks.
Presenting a vague plan without specific timings, assigned resources, or sequence of actions.
rules: A written narrative with a map is provided. Candidates get 10 minutes to read and write individual plans.
The group then discusses for 20 minutes to arrive at a common group plan.
All candidates must participate in the group discussion phase.
The group nominates one person to present the final group plan to the GTO.
Writing materials are provided for individual planning — candidates keep their written plans.

tasks.name: Lecturette
tasks.description: Each candidate delivers a short 3-minute lecture on one of four given topics. Tests the ability to organize thoughts quickly, speak confidently, and present ideas in a structured manner to an audience.
strategy: Pick the topic you know best — don't choose a 'impressive' topic you can't sustain for 3 minutes.
Structure your talk: Introduction (30s) → 2-3 Main Points (2 min) → Conclusion (30s).
Use the PEEL method for each point: Point, Explanation, Example, Link back to topic.
Maintain steady eye contact with the audience and use natural hand gestures.
End with a strong concluding statement — don't trail off with 'that's all' or 'thank you'.
commonMistakes: Running out of content after 1 minute because you didn't structure your talk beforehand.
Reading from notes the entire time instead of making eye contact with the audience.
Speaking too fast due to nervousness — practice controlled pacing and deliberate pauses.
Choosing a topic you know nothing about just because it sounds impressive.
Not managing time — going over 3 minutes or finishing too early both reflect poor planning.
rules: Four topic cards are placed face-down. The candidate picks one card and chooses one of the four topics.
Preparation time is approximately 3 minutes after selecting the topic.
The lecture duration is exactly 3 minutes. A bell rings at 2.5 minutes as a warning.
The candidate stands and addresses the group who are seated as the audience.
No notes or reference material can be used during the actual lecture delivery.

tasks.name: Progressive Group Task
tasks.description: The group faces a series of outdoor obstacles with increasing difficulty. Using limited helping materials (planks, ropes, etc.), the group must cross obstacles without touching the ground in restricted zones. Tests teamwork, planning, and progressive problem-solving.
strategy: Observe the obstacle setup completely before suggesting a plan — rushing leads to failed attempts.
Always account for the 'load rule' — materials and people must cross together efficiently.
Volunteer to go first on risky crossings to demonstrate courage, but don't be reckless.
Keep helping materials organized — track which planks and ropes are available at each stage.
Encourage struggling teammates vocally — the GTO watches for cooperative leadership, not solo heroics.
commonMistakes: Touching the ground or restricted zones (out-of-bounds areas) — this resets the entire obstacle.
Arguing with teammates about the approach instead of quickly testing and iterating.
Hoarding the leadership role — let others suggest ideas and build on them collectively.
Forgetting to bring helping materials forward — stranding them at a previous obstacle.
Giving up after a failed attempt instead of quickly regrouping and trying a different approach.
rules: The group receives a set of helping materials (planks, ropes, ballies) at the start.
Ground between start and finish is 'out of bounds' — touching it means starting that obstacle over.
All group members and all helping materials must cross each obstacle before moving to the next.
Obstacles become progressively harder — the first is a warm-up, the last requires full coordination.
The GTO may add time pressure or additional constraints as the task progresses.

tasks.name: Half Group Task
tasks.description: Similar to PGT but with the group split in half (4-5 candidates per sub-group). Each sub-group faces the same obstacles, allowing the GTO to observe candidates more closely. Ideal for candidates who were quiet during PGT.
strategy: Step up more actively than in PGT — with a smaller group, your contribution is more visible.
Take initiative to suggest the plan early — in a smaller group, hesitation is more noticeable.
Physically help teammates cross obstacles — hold planks steady, offer a hand, stabilize ropes.
Communicate clearly and concisely — there are fewer people, so every word matters more.
If you were quiet in PGT, this is your chance to demonstrate leadership and initiative.
commonMistakes: Assuming HGT is easier because the group is smaller — obstacles are equally challenging.
Not adjusting your strategy for fewer people — you have less manpower for load distribution.
Being passive and waiting for others to lead — with 4-5 people, everyone must contribute.
Ignoring the time constraint — 20 minutes goes fast with full obstacles to cross.
Not coordinating with your sub-group beforehand — brief planning saves execution time.
rules: The group is divided into two sub-groups of roughly equal size.
Each sub-group attempts the same set of obstacles simultaneously or in sequence.
Same ground rules as PGT — no touching restricted zones, all materials must cross.
Time limit is shorter than PGT, demanding faster decision-making.
The GTO specifically watches for candidates who step up more in the smaller group setting.

tasks.name: Command Task
tasks.description: Each candidate is appointed as commander and must lead 2-3 subordinates (chosen by the GTO) through an outdoor obstacle. The commander plans the approach, assigns roles, and directs execution. This is the most direct test of leadership ability.
strategy: Take 30-60 seconds to study the obstacle before announcing your plan — rushed plans fail.
Brief your subordinates clearly: 'You do X, you do Y, I will do Z. Let's start on my count.'
Stay calm and decisive — if plan A fails, immediately switch to plan B without showing frustration.
Position yourself where you can see the entire obstacle and direct traffic effectively.
Thank and encourage your subordinates — genuine leadership includes respect and motivation.
commonMistakes: Jumping into action without a plan — the GTO values planning before execution.
Treating subordinates rudely or barking orders — leadership is about influence, not authority.
Doing all the physical work yourself instead of delegating — you're the commander, not a laborer.
Panicking when the first attempt fails — composure under pressure is being directly tested.
Not using all available helping materials — overlooking a plank or rope that solves the obstacle.
rules: The GTO selects 2-3 candidates as your subordinates for the task.
The commander is briefed on the obstacle and has a few minutes to plan.
Only the commander gives instructions — subordinates follow the commander's directions.
The commander may also physically participate in crossing the obstacle.
The task must be completed within the allotted time. The GTO may ask the commander questions about the plan.

tasks.name: Final Group Task
tasks.description: The last outdoor group task, designed to give every candidate a final chance to demonstrate their abilities. The entire group works together on one obstacle. The GTO pays special attention to candidates who haven't stood out in previous tasks.
strategy: Give your absolute best effort — this is your last chance to make an impression in outdoor tasks.
Support teammates who haven't had much visibility — helping others shine reflects well on you.
Stay energetic and vocal throughout — the GTO notices candidates who maintain stamina.
If you've been quiet, take charge of at least one aspect: planning, materials, or encouragement.
Finish strong — the last impression matters as much as the first in GTO assessment.
commonMistakes: Relaxing because it's the 'final' task — this is when the GTO pays the most attention.
Being physically exhausted and showing it — maintain energy even if you're tired.
Not participating because you feel you've already done enough in earlier tasks.
Ignoring team members who are struggling — cooperation scores matter until the very end.
Rushing to finish without ensuring all materials and people have crossed properly.
rules: The entire group participates together — no sub-groups.
The obstacle difficulty is comparable to mid-level PGT obstacles.
Same ground rules apply — no touching restricted zones.
This is explicitly the last chance for candidates to demonstrate GTO qualities.
Time is strictly enforced — the group must complete the task within the limit.

tasks.name: Snake Race
tasks.description: Two sub-groups compete in a timed race across a series of obstacles while holding a snake-like structure (a long heavy log or plank). Tests group coordination, physical fitness, team spirit, and competitive drive under pressure.
strategy: Coordinate with your team before the race — assign positions based on height and strength.
Maintain rhythm while carrying the snake — out-of-sync movements slow everyone down.
Encourage your team vocally — war cries and motivation boost morale and impress the GTO.
Place the strongest members at the front and back for obstacle navigation.
Don't sacrifice safety for speed — injuries from reckless racing reflect poorly on judgment.
commonMistakes: Dropping the snake or log — this usually means restarting from the beginning.
Not communicating while navigating obstacles — silent teams trip over each other.
Focusing only on winning and ignoring team members who are struggling or falling behind.
Losing morale when the other team is ahead — the GTO values effort over outcome.
Poor positioning — placing shorter candidates in the middle where the weight is heaviest.
rules: The group is divided into two sub-groups for a competitive race.
Each sub-group carries a 'snake' (heavy log/plank) throughout the race.
The snake must be carried by all team members at all times — no one can let go.
The race involves crossing multiple obstacles: ditches, low walls, zigzag paths, etc.
The first team to cross the finish line with all members and the snake wins.

tasks.name: Individual Obstacles
tasks.description: Each candidate attempts a set of 10 physical obstacles individually within 3 minutes. Obstacles are numbered 1-10 in increasing difficulty and carry corresponding points. Tests physical fitness, courage, and self-confidence.
strategy: Practice the obstacles beforehand if possible — familiarity reduces hesitation at the actual test.
Start with obstacles you're confident about to build momentum — don't waste time on impossible ones.
Attempt at least 6-7 obstacles to show effort — the GTO values attempt over perfection.
Use proper technique: grip the ropes correctly, jump from the right foot, maintain body balance.
If you fail an obstacle, move to the next immediately — don't waste time on repeated attempts.
commonMistakes: Standing frozen at an obstacle out of fear — even a failed attempt is better than not trying.
Spending too much time on one difficult obstacle and missing easier ones later.
Not warming up before the test — cold muscles increase injury risk and reduce performance.
Attempting obstacles recklessly without technique — this leads to injuries and failed attempts.
Giving up after failing the first 2-3 obstacles instead of attempting the remaining ones.
rules: 10 obstacles are set up in a sequence, numbered 1 (easiest) to 10 (hardest).
Each candidate gets exactly 3 minutes to attempt as many obstacles as possible.
Candidates can attempt obstacles in any order — they don't have to go sequentially.
Each obstacle can only be attempted once — no second chances on the same obstacle.
Points are awarded based on the obstacle number (Obstacle 1 = 1 point, Obstacle 10 = 10 points).

tasks.name: Outdoor Group Tasks
tasks.description: A comprehensive outdoor session where the group faces a series of real-world simulated obstacles in an open field. Combines elements of PGT, material management, and team coordination. This is the core GTO outdoor testing phase.
strategy: Survey the entire course before starting — understanding the full scope helps with material planning.
Designate material handlers — someone should track available planks, ropes, and ballies at all times.
Rotate leadership naturally — don't try to lead every obstacle, let others step up too.
Stay hydrated and conserve energy — outdoor sessions are long and physically demanding.
Help the weakest team member — the GTO watches how the group treats its struggling members.
commonMistakes: Exhausting yourself on the first few obstacles and having nothing left for the harder ones.
Forgetting helping materials at previous obstacles — always do a material check before moving.
Not communicating the plan to the full group — whispering with 2-3 people leaves others excluded.
Ignoring the rules about restricted zones when the GTO isn't looking directly — they always see.
Celebrating early or relaxing between obstacles instead of maintaining focus and energy.
rules: The full group participates in all outdoor obstacles as a single team.
Helping materials are provided and must be carried throughout the course.
Standard ground rules apply — restricted zones cannot be touched.
The GTO may introduce new constraints or modify obstacles mid-task.
Total time is fixed — the group must manage pace to attempt all obstacles.

tasks.name: Helping Material Tasks
tasks.description: Focused tasks where the group must creatively use limited helping materials (planks, ropes, ballies, tin cans) to solve physical obstacles. Tests resourcefulness, planning, and the ability to see unconventional uses for standard tools.
strategy: Inventory all available materials before planning — know exact lengths of planks and ropes.
Think about materials as bridges, levers, anchors, and supports — not just in their obvious use.
Test your plan mentally before executing — imagine each step and check if materials reach.
Assign one person as 'material coordinator' to prevent confusion during execution.
Consider combining materials — two short planks can sometimes replace one long plank.
commonMistakes: Not measuring distances against plank lengths — assuming a plank will reach when it won't.
Using all materials for one obstacle and having nothing left for the next.
Not securing ropes properly — loose knots cause failures and waste time.
Ignoring creative solutions — sometimes the simplest approach with fewer materials is best.
Arguing about material allocation instead of quickly testing different configurations.
rules: A specific set of helping materials is provided at the start — no additional materials allowed.
All materials must be used within the rules — no modifying, breaking, or altering them.
The group must cross the obstacle using only the provided materials and their own bodies.
Materials cannot be thrown across obstacles — they must be carried or placed.
All materials must be retrieved after each obstacle for use in subsequent ones.

tasks.name: Personal Obstacles
tasks.description: Similar to Individual Obstacles but with a focus on personal physical challenges that test individual courage and willpower. Includes obstacles like commando crawl, balancing beam, jumping over walls, and rope climbing.
strategy: Build physical fitness weeks before SSB — regular running, pull-ups, and rope climbing help immensely.
Visualize each obstacle before attempting — mental rehearsal reduces anxiety and improves performance.
Use momentum to your advantage — don't stop between obstacles, keep moving to maintain flow.
Focus on technique over brute strength — proper form prevents injuries and improves success rate.
Attempt every obstacle even if you think you'll fail — the assessors value courage and attempt.
commonMistakes: Not building physical fitness before arriving at SSB — these obstacles require genuine strength.
Hesitating at height-based obstacles — showing visible fear is worse than falling after attempting.
Using incorrect grip or jumping technique that leads to injuries.
Comparing yourself to fitter candidates and losing confidence — focus on your own performance.
Skipping obstacles because they look too hard — attempt is always better than avoidance.
rules: Each candidate attempts obstacles individually while the group watches.
A fixed time limit is given per candidate (typically 3-5 minutes for all obstacles).
Obstacles can be attempted in any order within the time limit.
Safety is paramount — candidates must follow the demonstrated technique for each obstacle.
The GTO and physical instructor are present for safety oversight throughout.
